keep: The eye that knew in ten minutes which thing mattered was the same one that refused his daughter for years.
lede: He invented almost none of it. What he had was the ability to see, faster than anyone in the room, which thing was the one that mattered.
copy: In December 1979 he walked into Xerox PARC, and Apple had paid for the visit — Xerox was allowed to buy a hundred thousand pre-IPO shares for a million dollars. What he saw was the Alto: a graphical interface, already running. "I remember within ten minutes of seeing the graphical user interface stuff, just knowing that every computer would work this way some day," he told Daniel Morrow in 1995. The theft story misses the harder half. Bill Atkinson and Larry Tesler still had to invent the menu bar, overlapping windows, and a mouse cheap enough to put in a box.

He was not fired in 1985. In April the board backed John Sculley and stripped him of the Macintosh division while leaving him the chairman's title; he attempted a boardroom coup in May, lost, and resigned in September. He incorporated NeXT the same week. He also put ten million dollars into Lucasfilm's graphics group as it spun out in February 1986, five to Lucasfilm for the technology and five to run the company. That became Pixar, and Disney bought it for about $7.4 billion in 2006. Apple bought NeXT in 1997, and by September he was running the company again.

The refusal that shipped the products was not reserved for products. He denied paternity of his daughter Lisa in a 1980 filing that described him as sterile. A blood test put the probability of paternity at 94.4 per cent, by his daughter's own account, and he answered that this meant 28 per cent of American men could be her father — which is not what the number says. Diagnosed in October 2003 with a rare and unusually treatable pancreatic tumour, he tried diet and acupuncture for nine months before agreeing to surgery. Isaacson reports him saying he had not wanted his body opened, and hearing regret in the way he said it.

bio.t: Becoming Steve Jobs: The Evolution of a Reckless Upstart into a Visionary Leader
bio.why: Schlender covered him for twenty-five years and knew him, and the book is built on that access rather than on late interviews. Walter Isaacson's 'Steve Jobs' (2011) is the famous one and the more complete record; this is the one the people who worked with him point to.

contested: Which book you read decides which man you get. Isaacson had Jobs's cooperation and wrote the version everyone now quotes; Tim Cook has said publicly that it made him out to be a greedy egomaniac and did him a disservice, and Jony Ive and Eddy Cue have said much the same. The obvious answer to that objection is that all three worked for him. Malcolm Gladwell's 'Creation Myth' makes the sharper point about PARC: the failure worth studying is Xerox's inability to ship what its own researchers had built, not Apple's visit.

across.label: Compounding Machines
across.txt: — Xerox invented the personal computer and shipped almost none of it. This is the man who shipped it.
